Q: trying out openclaw in a VM A:

Running experimental or unfamiliar software inside a virtual machine is generally considered a safer approach compared to installing it directly on your main operating system. A VM creates an isolated environment, which helps limit potential damage if the software behaves unexpectedly.

If you are testing something like OpenClaw and are concerned about security or network access, using a VM with restricted permissions is usually a reasonable option. For example, you can disable shared folders, restrict clipboard sharing, and control network access.

Another common approach is using a VM with a NAT network configuration so the software does not have full access to the host network. This provides an extra layer of isolation.

However, if the tool requires deeper system access or interacts heavily with networking components, some developers prefer testing it on a separate remote server or a disposable cloud instance. This avoids any risk to the main machine or local network.

In general, a properly isolated VM is considered safe for testing most experimental tools, as long as standard security precautions are followed.

Q: Invoke-Sqlcmd times out after ~30s on some machines but not others (without -QueryTimeout). What determines the default and what’s best practice? A:

AlwaysLearning provided the crucial pointer in a comment on the question:

Your symptom suggests that different machines of yours use different editions of the Invoke-SqlCmd cmdlet:

There are two - technically distinct - Invoke-SqlCmd cmdlets:[1]

  • (a) The obsolete Invoke-SqlCmd command from the obsolete SQLPS module.

    • For the sake of backward compatibility, this obsolete module still comes with SSMS.

  • (b) The current Invoke-SqlCmd command from the successor module, SqlServer

    • Only v16.x versions of SSMS came bundled with this module.
    • In v17.x and above, it can be installed from the PowerShell Gallery with, e.g.: Install-Module -Scope CurrentUser SqlServer
      and later upgraded with, e.g.:
      Update-Module -Scope CurrentUser SqlServer

You can tell which version is loaded (implicitly) on a given machine by running the following command in a pristine session, which also reveals the originating module's version number:

(Get-Command Invoke-SqlCmd).Module

  • Implementation (a) de facto appears to default to 30 seconds.

    • The official help topic is, as of this writing, malformed and is missing a description of the -QueryTimeout parameter (a description of the command as a whole is presented instead).

    • It's hard to find definitive claims to that effect, but here's a pointer from Troubleshoot query time-out errors:

      • If the query doesn't return any data within the configured time-out value (typically 30 seconds)

  • By contrast, implementation (b) defaults to not timing out, based on the official help topic stating for the -QueryTimeout parameter:

    • If a timeout value is not specified, the queries do not time out.

    • Conceivably, an older version of the SqlServer module also had the 30-second timeout; if so, update to the latest version with, e.g.,
      Update-Module -Scope CurrentUser SqlServer

[1] See SQL Server PowerShell for background information.

Q: How do developers usually handle database optimization for growing WordPress sites? A:

First, make a backup and make sure you can restore it in case you fat-finger something. Even better, try out all these optimizations on a staging site before using them on a live site.

I wrote a free non-monetized plugin a few years ago to overcome the indexing efficiency difficulties caused by the need to support legacy versions of the MySql DBMS. It is seeing some success. https://wordpress.org/plugins/index-wp-mysql-for-speed/

It gets rid of the notorious prefix indexes that slow things down, especially in the meta tables.

There are several database-cleaning plugins. I like Younes JFR’S Advanced Database Cleaner. It can scrub out a lot of orphaned cruft and old post revisions. https://wordpress.org/plugins/advanced-database-cleaner/

Tables left behind by plugins you uninstalled? Here’s what I do.

  1. Open a support topic with the developer. We’re supposed to drop tables we created on uninstall. When we don’t it’s a defect.

  2. Use a SQL client (phpmyadmin) to say

    RENAME TABLE wp_old_plugin_table TO drop_me_old_plugin_table

    Then, a month later if everything is working right I DROP the table. If something breaks and the old table is still needed it’s easy to rename it back.

Another thing to consider: add a persistent object cache to reduce the database workload.

And ask your hosting provider to set these two directives in php.ini, to make php run WordPress more efficiently.

opcache.memory_utilization=256
opcache.interned_strings_buffer=24

Q: Safely validating AST of LLM-generated PostgreSQL queries in Java to prevent side effects A:

"JSQLParser is a RDBMS agnostic parser with a certain focus on SQL:2016 Standard compliant Queries". You'd have to build out JSQLParser to a point where it just re-implements Postgres' own parser, rewriter and optimiser, then connect it to the target db to be able to perform query validation deep enough to understand function bodies and the rewrite rule system. It makes a bit more sense to just re-use Postgres' code.

A good example is the Pgpool-II project where they faced this exact problem (the pool needs to understand the query tree in order re-route it to different databases in load balancing), and that's exactly how they solved it - instead of trying to do their own query processor, they simply started using the Postgres' original source code.

If you just want to detect and reject function calls, traverse the tree and search for expression types that are some sort of a function call. The links are for JSQLParser, but the process in Calcite should be similar.

Note that

  • Operators can also be defined with arbitrary, potentially unsafe logic
  • Tables can have functions in their column default and generated expressions - insert and update will cause a call, but merely selecting a column1 from yourtable can also lead to an invocation if it's defined as int generated always as (myfunct()) virtual.
  • View and materialized view definitions can have function and operator calls in them too. If you select x from myview, you'll call the function that generates x. If someone calls refresh materialized view mymatview, they can also invoke some functions.
  • There can be custom rules and triggers that fire in response to otherwise safe-looking SQL statements
  • RLS policies can quietly add function and operator calls to any statement targeting a specific object
  • Database users can overload functions and operators, making them invoke a different (set of) functions. If you plan to maintain an allowlist, it would have to include full signatures, not just names.
  • Which function/operator gets invoked depends on not just the argument types, but also caller's current search_path setting. You can have multiple completely different function with the same name and argument types, as long as they're located in different schemas. Signatures on the theoretical allowlist must be schema-qualified.

Good luck.

Q: Foldmethod=marker and syntax at the same time? A:

I placed this directly in my ../syntax/ruby.vim (before the "syn region rubyMultilineComment...")

syn region rubyMyFoldRegion   start="^\s*#[{][{]\ze\%(\s.*\)\=$" end="^\s*#[}][}]\%(\s.*\)\=$"    transparent keepend fold

Yes this is not the combination of two fold methods. It is just syntax.
But the result is what I wanted. So (my) next question is:
How to combine additional syntax with existing syntax files? (either to all or selected)
How to ensure, that the adds are inserted at the correct position?
